issues.explanation: 'Dogs' as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of this military trauma profile: the other triggers/threat items center on interpersonal danger from men, being watched, and sudden human movements, with no supporting memory/appraisal content linking animals to the trauma. This makes the dog trigger clinically incoherent within the selected five components.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links Threat → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers, but the other selected strategies (overworking, never being alone with another person) plausibly manage interpersonal threat and hypervigilance, whereas gambling does not map clearly onto the endorsed trigger/threat pattern and reads as addressing a different problem domain.

vignette:
Meera is a 66-year-old midwife who has spent over three decades delivering babies in a busy urban hospital. But the calm competence her colleagues see conceals a life organized around fear. That fear began during her military service decades ago, when she was deployed as a combat-zone midwife. One night, while attending a difficult labor in a makeshift clinic, her commanding officer-a tall man in a crisp uniform-stood in the doorway watching her. She was alone with him, and though he said nothing overtly threatening, his steady gaze and her sense of being trapped under his authority made her skin crawl. She finished the delivery in silence, but something in her shifted that night. She has never felt safe since.

Today, any male presence can ignite that old vigilance. At work, when a male obstetrician enters the delivery suite and stands near the door, her attention snaps away from the patient. She becomes hyperalert, scanning the room for exits, noticing every movement he makes. A sudden shift of his weight or a hand reaching for a chart puts her immediately on guard. She cannot relax even in the safe, sterile environment she knows rationally is secure. The sight of a security guard in uniform on the hospital's main floor triggers the same response: her heart pounds, her breath shortens, and she feels watched, as if the old watching is happening again.

This constant threat monitoring exhausts her, but she has learned one way to manage it: she throws herself into work. She takes on extra shifts, stays late to restock supplies, volunteers to cover colleagues' breaks. Keeping her mind occupied with tasks-checking fetal monitors, writing notes, washing instruments-helps crowd out the hypervigilance, at least for a while. She also makes sure she is never alone with another person, especially a man. When a male colleague asks for a private word, she finds a reason to leave the door open, or she says she needs to check on a patient immediately. She arranges her lunch breaks to coincide with crowded periods in the staff room, and she waits in hallways until someone else is around to join her before entering a supply closet. These strategies feel necessary, but they have a cost: the more she overworks and the more she avoids solitude, the more often she finds herself in situations that trigger her fear. Staying busy means being present in more moments where male doctors or orderlies are nearby. Avoiding being alone means she is always in places where people are watching her-patients, nurses, visitors-and that sense of being observed only amplifies her vigilance. She is caught in a loop she cannot see.

Over the months, a consequence has taken hold: her husband, Ajay, has noticed she no longer sits with him in the living room at night. Instead she stands by the kitchen counter, folding laundry or reviewing her schedule, too keyed up to settle. He has gently asked if something is wrong, but she cannot explain. What finally brought Meera to seek help was an incident last week. A new male nurse, young and earnest, asked her to step into an empty consultation room to discuss a patient. She found herself frozen, her mouth dry, and she abruptly walked out without a word. That night she did not sleep. She called her primary care doctor the next morning. What scares her most now is the possibility that she will lose her ability to do the work she loves-and that the watching will never stop.
